Text:
Physics is usually divided into two fields:

motion, fluids, heat, sound, light, electricity, magnetism → {{c1::classical::classical/modern}} physics

relativity, atomic structure, quantum theory, condensed matter, nuclear physics, elementary particles, cosmology and astrophysics → {{c1::modern::classical/modern}} physics
Back Extra:
Why: physics is the most basic of the sciences — it deals with the behavior and structure of matter.

Cue: the study of motion is also called mechanics.

Text: Aristotle, who argued that rest is the natural state of objects, lived {{c1::384–322 B.C.::lifespan}}, and Galileo, the first true experimentalist, lived {{c2::1564–1642::lifespan}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: Aristotle watched pushed objects slow and stop, so rest seemed natural; Galileo imagined frictionless motion continuing forever, and so founded our modern view of motion.

Cue: nearly 1,900 years separate them — B.C. antiquity to the Renaissance.

Text: In science, a theory is {{c1::a broad, testable explanation that orders observations}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Observation, with careful experimentation and measurement, is one side of the scientific process. The other side is the invention or creation of theories to explain and order the observations."

Distinguish: a model is a simple analogy to the familiar; a law is a concise statement of how nature behaves — a theory is the broader explanatory picture.

Why: theories are never derived directly from observations — they are inspirations of the human mind, accepted or rejected by observation and experiment.

Text: The notebooks of {{c1::Leonardo da Vinci}} contain the first references to {{c2::the forces acting within a structure}} — a subject regarded as physics today, with great relevance to architecture and building.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: da Vinci (1452–1519) worked a century before Galileo (1564–1642), the first true experimentalist.

Why: the development of physics has both influenced and been influenced by other fields.

Ex: early work on electricity, leading to the battery and electric current, came from Luigi Galvani — an eighteenth-century physiologist.

Text: In science, a {{c1::model}} is {{c2::an analogy to something already familiar}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a theory is broader, more detailed, and gives quantitatively testable predictions — a model only offers structural similarity to the phenomena.

Why: the purpose of a model is an approximate mental or visual picture — something to hold on to — when we cannot see what is actually happening.

Ex: the wave model of light — we cannot see light waves, but light behaves in many respects as water waves do.

Text: A scientific {{c1::law}} is {{c2::a concise but general statement}} about how nature behaves, often taking the form of {{c3::a relationship or equation between quantities}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a principle is the same kind of statement but less general; a theory is a broader, more detailed picture of the phenomena.

Ex: conservation of electric charge; Newton's second law, F = ma.

Pitfall: scientific laws are descriptive — they say how nature does behave; political laws are prescriptive — how we ought to behave.

Text: In science, a principle is {{c1::a statement like a law, but less general}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "For less general statements, the term principle is often used (such as Archimedes' principle)."

Distinguish: a law is experimentally valid over a wide range of observed phenomena — charge conservation, F = ma; a principle covers a narrower range.
